claims.text: Percolating chemical short-range-order clusters in single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys cause a non-monotonic transition in thermal conductivity.
Isolated SRO clusters reduce thermal conductivity through increased phonon scattering.
Once SRO clusters percolate, thermal conductivity increases or remains anomalously high.
A percolating SRO network creates coherent, low-scattering phonon channels that bypass standard mixing limits.
HfNbTaTiZr and MoNbTaW are examples of bcc refractory high-entropy-alloy solid solutions.
Near-equiatomic multicomponent HEA solid solutions have high configurational entropy.
MoNbTaW can exhibit a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering.
The proposed initial state has substantial SRO driving force but lacks long-range order.
Controlled annealing or rapid quenching can evolve SRO from isolated clusters into a percolating network while retaining a single bcc phase.
The alloy remains single-phase bcc above 0.5 Tm.
Standard empirical potentials such as EAM fail to capture the relevant SRO energetics or evolution.
A highly accurate machine-learning interatomic potential has been used to simulate SRO effects in bcc MoNbTaW.
Percolation of ordered clusters shifts phonon transport from diffuse scattering at isolated clusters to coherent propagation through ordered domains.
Connected ordered pathways reduce the effective disorder potential for selected phonon modes and thereby mitigate scattering.
Simple series-parallel mixing rules and Debye-Callaway-type baselines predict a monotonic decrease in conductivity with increasing SRO.
Thermal conductivity should show a knee or inflection and then increase or plateau when SRO correlation length exceeds the phonon mean free path.
HEAs can decompose into multiple phases as composition or annealing temperature changes.
AlCoFeNi is an example in which decomposition or an ordered-phase transition occurs.
The magnitude of the conductivity increase depends strongly on the accuracy of the modeled potential-energy surface.
The hypothesis can be tested by jointly measuring simulated thermal conductivity, SRO correlation length, and cluster connectivity across the percolation transition.
